summary: Describes YANG mechanisms for defining abstract data structures, meaning structures that are not part of a configuration datastore. For example, they can describe message contents.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language network devices use to describe their settings and their state. This document adds a way to use YANG for something else: describing the shape of data that is neither, such as the contents of a protocol message.

questions: how to define abstract data structures in yang
what is the yang structure extension
subtitle: Two YANG extensions for defining abstract data structures that are not configuration or operational state.

tldr.problem: Protocol messages and files need to be described in YANG without being configuration or state, and the older yang-data extension was limited and hard to extend.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a structure extension to declare an abstract data structure, and an augment-structure extension to add nodes to one from another module.
tldr.outcome: Specifications can model whole or nested messages and let external documents extend them, using the same tree-diagram and encoding conventions as other YANG data.

today: RFC 8791 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 8340 with the tree-diagram sections for structures.

sections.title: Why a New Structure Statement
sections.content:
There is a need for standard mechanisms that allow the definition of abstract data that is not intended to be implemented as configuration or operational state. The 'yang-data' extension statement from RFC 8040 was defined for this purpose, but it is limited in its functionality.

The intended use of 'yang-data' was to model all or part of a protocol message, such as the 'errors' definition in the YANG module 'ietf-restconf' in RFC 8040, or the contents of a file. However, protocols are often layered such that the header or payload portions of the message can be extended by external documents, and the YANG statements that model a protocol need to support that extensibility, which already exists in the protocol itself.

This document defines a new YANG extension statement called 'structure', which is similar to but more flexible than 'yang-data'. There is no assumption that a YANG data structure can only be used as a top-level abstraction, and it may also be nested within some other data structure. It also defines a new extension statement called 'augment-structure', which allows abstract data structures to be augmented from external modules and is similar to the existing YANG 'augment' statement. The ordinary 'augment' statement cannot be used to augment a YANG data structure, because a YANG compiler or other tool is not required to understand the 'structure' extension.

The point of the two extensions is that a data structure can be described once, in the document that owns it, and then extended by other documents without the extending document needing to change the original one.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is the language network devices use to describe their settings and their state. This document adds a way to use YANG for something else: describing the shape of data that is neither, such as the contents of a protocol message.

sections.title: The Term YANG Data Structure
sections.content:
The document introduces one term of its own. A YANG data structure is a data structure defined with the 'structure' statement.

The terms configuration and operational state come from the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342) and are not redefined. The terms absolute-schema-nodeid, container, data definition statement, data node, leaf, leaf-list and list come from RFC 7950 and are not redefined either.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines one term: a YANG data structure is data described with the new structure statement. Everything else it uses comes from the main YANG specification.

sections.title: Defining and Encoding a Data Structure
sections.content:
A YANG data structure is defined with the 'structure' extension statement, which is defined in the YANG module 'ietf-yang-structure-ext'. The argument to the statement is the name of the data structure. The data structures share the same identifier namespace as the data definition statements of RFC 7950, so a data structure cannot have the same name as a sibling node from a regular data definition statement, or as another 'structure' statement, in the same module.

Defining a structure does not force it to be used as a top-level protocol message or other top-level data structure. A YANG data structure is encoded in the same way as an 'anydata' node: the name of the structure is encoded as a container, with the instantiated children encoded as child nodes of it. So a structure called my-error with a child leaf error-number of type int is encoded in JSON as an object named for the module and the structure, holding the leaf value.

Two data definition statements are constrained inside a 'structure' statement. The list statement is not required to have a key statement, and the config statement is ignored if present. The XPath document element is the extension statement itself, so the child nodes of the document element are the data definition substatements within it, and that conceptual document is the context for statements such as must, when, path, min-elements, max-elements, mandatory, unique and ordered-by, and for the instance-identifier data type.
sections.plainLanguage: A structure gets a name and its own set of nodes, and it shares the name space with the rest of the module so nothing can collide. When the structure appears in a document, its name behaves like a container holding the child nodes.

sections.title: Printing Structures in Tree Diagrams
sections.content:
A YANG data structure can be printed in a YANG tree diagram. This document updates RFC 8340 by defining two new sections in the tree diagram for a module.

The first is for YANG data structures. They are offset by two spaces and identified by the keyword 'structure' followed by the name of the structure and a colon. The second is for YANG data structure augmentations, offset by two spaces and identified by the keyword 'augment-structure' followed by the augment target structure name and a colon. Nodes in the structures are printed according to the rules in Section 2.6 of RFC 8340, and they do not have any flags.

The tree diagram of the address-book example in the RFC therefore looks like this: a 'structure address-book' line, then a list of addresses keyed on last and first, with leaves for last, first, street, city and state, the last three being optional.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG has a usual way of drawing the shape of a module as an indented tree. The document adds two more kinds of line to that drawing, one for structures and one for the things added to a structure from another module.

sections.title: The Two Extension Statements
sections.content:
The 'structure' extension is used to specify a YANG data structure that represents conceptual data defined in YANG. It is intended to describe hierarchical data independent of protocol context or specific message encoding format, and the data definition statements within it specify the generic syntax for that structure, whose name is the argument of the statement. The extension does not define a media type: a specification using it MUST specify the message encoding rules, including the content media type, if applicable.

The 'structure' extension is only valid as a top-level statement, given as a substatement to 'module' or 'submodule'. Its substatements MUST follow the ABNF: a must statement, optional status, description and reference statements, any number of typedef or grouping statements, and any number of data definition statements. The module name and namespace value of the module using the extension are assigned to each of the resulting data definition statements.

The 'augment-structure' extension specifies an augmentation to a YANG data structure defined with the 'structure' statement. It has almost the same structure as the 'augment' statement. The mandatory 'path' argument identifies the conceptual data node being augmented and is represented as an absolute-schema-nodeid string, where the first node identifies the YANG data structure to augment and the rest identifies the node within the structure. It is also only valid as a top-level statement. Its substatements MUST be optional status, description and reference statements, followed by one or more data definition or case statements. The same two data definition statements are constrained: a list is not required to have a key, and the config statement is ignored.

The RFC's worked example defines an address book with a list of addresses, and then a second module that adds county and zipcode leaves to it with 'augment-structure', pointing at the path of the address list inside the structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The first extension declares a structure and says what may go inside it. The second adds nodes to a structure that somebody else declared, by giving the path of the node to extend. Both can only appear at the top level of a module.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-structure-ext in the 'ns' subregistry of the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant contact, and the note that the requested URI is an XML namespace.

IANA has also registered the YANG module 'ietf-yang-structure-ext' in the 'YANG Module Names' subregistry of the 'YANG Parameters' registry, with the same namespace, the prefix 'sx', and RFC 8791 as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The XML namespace list and the list of YANG module names each get one new entry for this document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines YANG extensions that are used to define conceptual YANG data structures. It does not introduce any new vulnerabilities beyond those specified in YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950).
sections.plainLanguage: Describing data shapes adds no risk of its own. The usual YANG security considerations still apply.

viz.caption: RULES THAT APPLY INSIDE A STRUCTURE

items.title: Shared names
items.text: A structure shares the identifier namespace of the module, so no sibling may have the same name.

items.title: Encoding
items.text: The structure is encoded the same way as an anydata node: its name becomes a container.

items.title: Context node
items.text: The XPath document element is the extension statement itself.

items.title: Statements that apply
items.text: must, when, path, min-elements, max-elements, mandatory, unique and ordered-by, and the instance-identifier type.

items.title: Two exceptions
items.text: A list needs no key statement, and the config statement is ignored.

data.title: An address book structure

viz.caption: TREE DIAGRAM OF THE EXAMPLE STRUCTURE (RFC 8791, APPENDIX A.1)

data.title: Tree diagram
data.code:
module: example-module

  structure address-book:
    +-- address* [last first]
       +-- last      string
       +-- first     string
       +-- street?   string
       +-- city?     string
       +-- state?    string
